William Mullins was a shoemaker of Dorking in Surrey, where the house he sold in 1619,
the year before the voyage, still stands.
He brought his wife Alice, his children Priscilla and Joseph, a servant, and a stock to trade.
He was dying before the first houses were up.
His will, taken down on board and witnessed by Governor Carver, the ship’s surgeon and the Mayflower’s master,
Christopher Jones, is among the first made in New England: “I have twenty-one dozen of shoes and thirteen pair of
boots, which I give into the Company’s hands for forty pounds”, and to “my daughter Priscilla ten pounds”.
He died on 21 February 1621. Bradford wrote the rest thirty years later: “Mister Mullins,
and his wife, his son, and his servant, died the first winter.
Only his daughter Priscilla survived, and married with John Alden, who are both living,
and have eleven children.” Their eldest, Elizabeth, married William Pabodie and lived into her ninety-third year at
Little Compton, Rhode Island. Tradition calls her the first English girl born at Plymouth,
though nothing from her own time says so.
The Boston News-Letter’s notice of her death in 1717 ended: “She has left a numerous posterity.
Her granddaughter, Bradford, is a grandmother.”
Elizabeth’s daughter Rebecca married William Southworth.
